claims.text: The investigated material is a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating on a Cu matrix with a disordered solid-solution structure.
The coating has high elastic modulus and stable wear resistance at 300 K.
At 300 K, strong lattice distortion restricts dislocation mobility.
The critical mechanism transition occurs above approximately 600 K.
The Cu substrate facilitates thermal conduction but does not suppress intrinsic thermal softening of the coating.
Increasing temperature changes deformation from isolated dislocation slip to dense stacking-fault networks and eventually severe lattice disorder or amorphization.
At low temperature, high-entropy lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion and promotes stable plasticity through limited slip.
Rising temperature thermally activates the nucleation and multiplication of stacking faults and dislocation loops.
At a critical temperature, the sluggish-diffusion effect is overcome and rapid defect accumulation begins.
Stacking faults and dislocation loops coalesce into amorphous-like regions.
Coalescence of stacking faults causes local lattice softening and reduces the effective elastic modulus.
Rapid lattice disorder and modulus loss trigger catastrophic deterioration in wear resistance.
A sharp decline in wear resistance and elastic modulus is likely between 600 K and 750 K.
The predicted decline coincides with an increase in stacking-fault density.
Above the threshold, the material loses the ability to sustain high contact stress without amorphization.
The baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating has high stacking-fault energy at 300 K.
The proposed mechanism applies specifically when the FeNiCrCoCu system is FCC-dominant.
Al-containing HEAs with significant BCC phase fractions have different high-temperature hardening mechanisms.
Molecular-dynamics simulations of CoCrFeNiMn show amorphization at very small grain sizes or high temperatures.
Direct high-temperature data on dislocation evolution in the specific FeNiCrCoCu-on-Cu system are lacking.
